Exact certificates with Z3

Source: vignettes/exact-certificates.Rmd
exact-certificates.Rmd
library(optcompR)

optcompR describes an optimization problem once, as variables, expressions, constraints and an objective, and then classifies it, chooses a capable solver

Numerical solvers work in floating point with tolerances. For linear models (LP and MILP) the z3r package gives access to Z3, whose linear integer and real arithmetic is a decision procedure: its answers sat and unsat are exact statements about the model as written.

These functions need z3r and the Z3 library (remotes::install_github("adamrsophie/z3r")).

Exact feasibility 

m <- opt_model()
x <- opt_variable(m, "x", type = "integer", lower = 0, upper = 10)
opt_constraint(m, 2 * x == 7)
opt_z3_check(m)
#> $status
#> [1] "unsat"
#> 
#> $values
#> NULL

No integer solves 2x = 7, and Z3 proves it. A satisfying assignment is a feasible point, not an optimal one:

m2 <- opt_model()
x <- opt_variable(m2, "x", type = "integer", lower = 0, upper = 10)
y <- opt_variable(m2, "y", lower = 0)
opt_constraint(m2, 2 * x + 0.1 * y == 7)
opt_objective(m2, y)
opt_z3_check(m2)
#> $status
#> [1] "sat"
#> 
#> $values
#>  x  y 
#>  0 70
opt_z3_check(m2, objective_bound = 9.99)$status
#> [1] "unsat"

The second call proves that no feasible point has y \le 9.99: because x \le 3 is forced, y = 70 - 20x \ge 10.

Certifying an optimum

opt_z3_certify() asks whether any feasible point beats the solver’s objective by more than a tiny relative margin. unsat proves the reported value optimal for the model.

k <- opt_model("max")
a <- opt_variable(k, "a", type = "binary")
b <- opt_variable(k, "b", type = "integer", lower = 0, upper = 3)
opt_constraint(k, a + b <= 4)
opt_objective(k, 3 * a + 2 * b)
r <- opt_solve(k)
opt_z3_certify(r)$certified
#> [1] TRUE

If the reported value were wrong, Z3 returns a better point as a counterexample:

bad <- r
bad$objective_value <- 8
opt_z3_certify(bad)[c("certified", "better_point")]
#> $certified
#> [1] FALSE
#> 
#> $better_point
#> a b 
#> 1 3

Coefficients

Coefficients are doubles. With coefficients = "decimal" (the default), 0.1 means exactly 1/10; with "binary" it means the exact binary value of the double, 3602879701896397 / 2^{55}.

What Z3 is not used for

Only linear models are translated. Z3’s nonlinear real arithmetic is incomplete and its semantics differ from numerical optimization, so quadratic and nonlinear models are refused rather than sent to Z3. Certification proves the optimal value, not exact feasibility of the floating point solution vector. Exact solving can be slow for large integer models.
